title: How do you build stable locators when the app generates dynamic IDs/attributes: prefer user-facing, accessibility-based locators (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByText`, `getByTestId`) over brittle CSS/XPath tied to generated values: and why do stable locators reduce flakiness and maintenance?
shortTitle: Building stable locators when the app generates dynamic IDs
keyPoints: Dynamic IDs and class names change on every build, so selectors tied to them break constantly, producing locator rot
getByRole finds elements by accessible role and name, mirroring how users perceive controls, and is the most reliable and accessibility-aligned
getByLabel finds form fields by their associated label text, ideal for inputs since users identify fields by labels
getByTestId uses a deliberate stable test attribute as a contract between developers and testers for elements with no semantic handle
Stable locators reduce flakiness because they depend on meaning, not markup, and reduce maintenance because a UI refactor does not break them
Preference order: getByRole first, then getByLabel, then getByText, then getByTestId, and raw CSS or XPath only as a last resort

s1_definition.oneliner: Locate elements by their user-facing meaning with getByRole, getByLabel, and getByText, and add a stable getByTestId where needed, instead of tying selectors to generated IDs or CSS, because meaning is stable while implementation details churn, which cuts flakiness and maintenance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Dynamic IDs** – Frameworks generate class names and element IDs at build or render time, so selectors tied to them break on every build.
- **getByRole** – Finds by accessible role and name (button, heading, textbox), mirroring how users and screen readers perceive controls. Most reliable.
- **getByLabel** – Finds form fields by their associated label text, ideal for inputs.
- **getByText** – Finds by visible text, appropriate when the words are the real identifier.
- **getByTestId** – Uses a deliberate stable attribute as a contract for elements with no semantic handle.
- **Preference order** – getByRole > getByLabel > getByText > getByTestId > raw CSS/XPath as last resort.
s1_definition.analogy: On the National Bank of India transfer screen, the sign-in button might be generated with a random internal identifier like "btn-9f3a2" that changes every rebuild. If the robot looks for that exact random name, it breaks the next day. Instead the robot finds the button the way Rajesh does: "the button that says Sign In." That meaning does not change when developers reshuffle the code.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Locator Preference Order
  ────────────────────────

  Priority 1: getByRole
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ button, heading, link, textbox,  │
  │ checkbox, alert, navigation      │
  │ Most reliable + accessible       │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
           │ if no role fits
           ▼
  Priority 2: getByLabel
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Form fields by their label text  │
  │ Best for inputs and selects      │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
           │ if no label
           ▼
  Priority 3: getByText
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Content, messages, unique links  │
  │ Risk: text changes for marketing │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
           │ if no unique text
           ▼
  Priority 4: getByTestId
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Deliberate stable attribute      │
  │ Contract: devs + testers agree   │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
           │ last resort
           ▼
  Priority 5: CSS / XPath
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Fragile, scope tightly           │
  │ Avoid if possible                │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When an application generates dynamic IDs and class names, any selector tied to those generated values breaks on every build, so I never pin locators to implementation details. Instead I locate elements by their meaning, which rarely changes. My preference order is: getByRole first because it is the most reliable and accessibility-aligned, then getByLabel for form fields, then getByText for content, then getByTestId as a deliberate stable contract for elements with no semantic handle, and raw CSS or XPath only as a scoped last resort.

Stable locators reduce flakiness because much of what looks like timing flakiness is actually locator rot, a selector that intermittently matches the wrong element or stops matching after a markup change. They reduce maintenance because a UI refactor does not break them as long as the button is still a button named "Transfer." And they improve accessibility by nudging the application toward correct roles and labels.

At the National Bank of India our app regenerated element IDs on every build, and the original suite, pinned to those IDs and nth-child paths, failed constantly. I rewrote the page objects using getByRole and getByLabel, added a small set of agreed test identifiers, and worked with developers to expose proper roles and labels. The flakiness dropped sharply and tests stopped needing edits after each release.

Remember one sentence: locate elements by their meaning with getByRole, getByLabel, and getByText, not by generated IDs, because meaning is stable while markup churns.
